newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich moves aggressively to restore party ties.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich moves aggressively to restore party ties.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich is in campaign mode: running hard to repair his battered image with Republican critics who have dismissed him as political roadkill and called for fresh leadership.

The House did little business this week but Gingrich went into damage-control overdrive. On issues ranging from death to taxes, he missed few opportunities to try to reassure restive conservatives he was back in their fold.

The Georgia Republican this week called for eliminating capital gains and estate taxes, soothing some Republicans who worried he was backing away from his commitment to a major tax cut after he said he might be willing to delay it.

"We are going to have a tax cut this year, we hope the president will sign it," Gingrich said. "We favour very low taxes, we favour abolishing the tax on savings and job creation, we favour abolishing the tax on death benefits."

He vowed to kill the National Endowment for the Arts -- a pet peeve of the conservative movement -- taking a swipe at rich Hollywood elites who he said come to Washington with their hands out for federal aid. The speaker got a dose of criticism himself for meeting with some stars, including actor Alec Baldwin, to discuss arts funding last month.

Gingrich, who was called "political roadkill" by New York Republican Representative Peter King, held forth before the Republican caucus and talked privately with 11 Republican renegades who embarrassed House leaders last month by voting to block legislation to pay for a probe into Democratic fund raising.
The lawmakers brought down the bill to send a message that they were fed up with what they termed a drift in the House and lack of commitment to balancing the budget.
"Lovefest might be a good way to put it," Arizona Republican Representative Matt Salmon said of Wednesday's meeting at which he said Gingrich's "demeanor was one of humility."
"I think he mended some fences, but the proof is in the pudding," Salmon said.
"I did hear many positive comments from Newt Gingrich," Wisconsin Republican Mark Neumann said. "He's beginning to say some very Republican-sounding things."

Gingrich has also been trying to capitalise on his recent trip to Asia, where he vowed the United States would defend Taiwan from any Chinese attack and got positive reviews from major newspapers. He held a bipartisan news conference to discuss Asia policy and reported on the trip in a speech to the House this week.

But Gingrich still has not said how he plans to pay a $300,000 penalty levied by the House ethics committee in January. He was reprimanded by the full House for ethics violations -- the first sitting speaker so punished.

Asked this week whether the speaker should pay the fine out of his own pocket, House Majority Leader Dick Armey, the No. 2 Republican, angrily told reporters: "You will have to discuss that with the speaker. I do not discuss that with him." Armey said Democrats, facing their own fund-raising scandal, should lay off Gingrich.

Lawmakers say that unless the House, which has moved at a sluggish pace, soon gets down to business, grumbling is sure to start up again. An emergency spending bill set for later this month will be a first test of budget-cutting resolve.
Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt said Thursday the House had done little substantive business this year and accused Gingrich of pandering to the right to keep his job.

"While we are not doing the work that we were sent here to do, it appears the speaker is trying to rehabilitate himself with the right wing of the Republican party by ... suggesting what I think its an outrageous tax proposal," Gephardt said.

Even Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, poured cold water on Gingrich's plans, saying he was hopeful for a capital gains and estate tax cut, but added: "I don't think we'll be able to eliminate them in one year."
